notes.definition: Fossils are the 'remains' of organisms from millions of years ago, which are found in rocks. They can form from parts that did not decay, from parts replaced by minerals, or as preserved traces such as footprints.
explanation: Fossils are the remains of organisms from millions of years ago, found in rocks. They are an important source of evidence about the history of life on Earth. There are three main ways that fossils can form, and you need to be able to describe all three.

First, fossils may form from parts of organisms that have not decayed because one or more of the conditions needed for decay are absent. Decay is carried out by microorganisms (decomposers), which need warmth, moisture and oxygen. If one of these is missing, decay stops or is very slow. Examples include woolly mammoths preserved in frozen ground (too cold), insects trapped in amber, which is hardened tree resin that keeps out oxygen and moisture, and bodies preserved in peat bogs, which are acidic and very low in oxygen.

Second, fossils may form when parts of the organism are replaced by minerals as they decay. This is the most common type of fossil. The organism dies and is quickly buried in sediment such as mud or sand. Soft parts decay quickly, but hard parts such as bones, shells and teeth decay slowly. As they decay, they are gradually replaced by minerals from water seeping through the sediment. Over millions of years the sediment turns into rock and a rock-like copy of the hard parts remains.

Third, fossils may be preserved traces of organisms rather than the organisms themselves. Examples are footprints, burrows and rootlet traces. For instance, a footprint left in soft mud may be filled with sediment and harden into rock. Trace fossils tell scientists about how organisms lived and moved, even if no body parts were preserved.

Many early forms of life were soft-bodied, which means they have left few traces behind, because soft tissue decays quickly and is rarely replaced by minerals. What traces there were have been mainly destroyed by geological activity, such as rocks being folded, worn away (eroded), or melted. This is why scientists cannot be certain about how life began on Earth, and why there are gaps in the fossil record.

We can learn from fossils how much or how little different organisms have changed as life developed on Earth. Rock layers are usually laid down with the oldest at the bottom, so fossils in deeper layers are generally older. Some organisms, such as sharks, have changed very little over hundreds of millions of years, while others have changed a great deal. Scientists use fossil data, together with classification data for living organisms, to draw evolutionary trees, which show how they believe organisms are related. On an evolutionary tree, the closer the branch point is to the present, the more recently two groups shared a common ancestor and the more closely related they are.
keyFacts: Fossils are the remains of organisms from millions of years ago, found in rocks.
Fossils can form from parts that have not decayed because one or more conditions for decay are absent (e.g. frozen, in amber, in peat bogs).
Fossils can form when parts of the organism are replaced by minerals as they decay (e.g. bones, shells, teeth).
Fossils can be preserved traces of organisms, such as footprints, burrows and rootlet traces.
Decay needs warmth, moisture and oxygen for microorganisms.
Early life forms were mostly soft-bodied, so they left few traces.
Many traces were destroyed by geological activity, so we cannot be certain how life began.
Fossils show how much or how little organisms have changed over time.
Deeper rock layers are usually older.
Evolutionary trees use classification data for living organisms and fossil data for extinct organisms.

keyTerms.definition: The remains of an organism from millions of years ago, found in rocks.
A preserved sign of an organism's activity, such as a footprint, burrow or rootlet trace, rather than the organism itself.
The gradual replacement of the parts of an organism by minerals as they decay, forming a rock-like copy.
The breakdown of dead material by microorganisms, which need warmth, moisture and oxygen.
Small particles such as mud and sand that settle in layers and can bury organisms; over time they form sedimentary rock.
All the fossils that have been found, arranged in order of age. It is incomplete.
A diagram showing how scientists believe organisms are related, based on classification data for living organisms and fossil data for extinct ones.
An ancestral species from which two or more later species evolved; shown as a branch point on an evolutionary tree.

workedExamples.title: Reading an evolutionary tree
workedExamples.question: On an evolutionary tree, species D and E branch apart 5 million years ago. Species A and B branch apart 20 million years ago. Which pair is more closely related, and how many years earlier did A and B split than D and E?
steps: The more recent the branch point, the more recent the common ancestor, so the more closely related the species.
D and E share a common ancestor from 5 million years ago, which is more recent than 20 million years ago.
workedExamples.answer: D and E are more closely related. A and B split 15 million years earlier.

workedExamples.title: Estimating the age of a fossil from rock layers
workedExamples.question: Sediment builds up in a lake at an average rate of 2 cm every 1000 years. A fossil is found 3 m below the top of the sediment. Estimate the age of the fossil.
steps: Convert to the same units: 3 m = 300 cm.
workedExamples.answer: About 150 000 years old (this is an estimate because the rate may not have been constant).

workedExamples.title: Identifying how a fossil formed
workedExamples.question: Say how each fossil formed: (a) a beetle trapped in amber; (b) a dinosaur bone made of stone; (c) a dinosaur footprint in rock.
steps: (a) Amber keeps out oxygen and moisture, so decay conditions are absent and the beetle did not decay.
(b) The bone was replaced by minerals as it slowly decayed.
(c) A footprint is a preserved trace of the organism, not part of its body.
workedExamples.answer: (a) Conditions for decay absent. (b) Replaced by minerals. (c) Preserved trace.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think all fossils are bones that have been preserved unchanged.
misconceptions.right: In fact, most bone fossils are rock-like copies where the bone was replaced by minerals. Fossils can also be unchanged remains (in ice or amber) or traces such as footprints.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think fossils of every organism that ever lived can be found.
misconceptions.right: In fact, most organisms never fossilised, especially soft-bodied ones, and many fossils were destroyed by geological activity, so the record has gaps.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the fossil record shows exactly how life began.
misconceptions.right: In fact, early life was soft-bodied and left few traces, so scientists cannot be certain how life began.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think species at the top of an evolutionary tree evolved from the species next to them.
misconceptions.right: In fact, living species at the tips share common ancestors at the branch points; one living species did not evolve from another living species.

realWorld: Woolly mammoths have been found frozen in Siberian permafrost, preserved because it was too cold for decay.
Insects millions of years old are found perfectly preserved in amber, which is used to study ancient ecosystems.
Dinosaur footprints (trace fossils) on beaches such as those on the Isle of Skye and the Jurassic Coast tell scientists how dinosaurs walked.
examTips: Learn all three ways fossils form, with an example of each: decay conditions absent (amber, ice, peat), replaced by minerals (bones, shells), traces (footprints, burrows, rootlet traces).
When explaining why decay did not happen, name the missing condition: oxygen, moisture or warmth.
For 'why can scientists not be certain how life began', give both reasons: early life was soft-bodied and left few traces, and geological activity destroyed traces.
On evolutionary trees, find the most recent branch point linking two species: the more recent it is, the more closely related they are.
When estimating ages from sediment, convert units first (m to cm) and remember that the answer is only an estimate.
summary: Fossils are remains of organisms from millions of years ago, found in rocks.
They form when decay conditions are absent, when parts are replaced by minerals, or as preserved traces.
Early soft-bodied life left few traces, and geological activity destroyed many, so the origin of life is uncertain.
Fossils show how much or how little organisms have changed over time.
Evolutionary trees show how organisms are believed to be related, using fossil and classification data.

It is too cold for decay to happen.

flashcards.front: Which parts are usually replaced by minerals?
flashcards.back: Hard parts such as bones, shells and teeth.

flashcards.front: Why did early life forms leave few fossils?

questions.question: Which statement best describes fossils?
options: Rocks shaped like animals by the wind
The remains of organisms from millions of years ago, found in rocks
Bones of animals that died in the last hundred years
markScheme: 1 mark: the remains of organisms from millions of years ago, found in rocks
questions.explanation: Fossils are remains of organisms from millions of years ago in rocks. Recent bones are not fossils, and rocks shaped by wind are not the remains of organisms.

questions.question: Which of these is a trace fossil?
markScheme: 1 mark: a dinosaur footprint in rock
questions.explanation: A trace fossil is a sign of an organism's activity, not part of its body. Shells, frozen mammoths and insects in amber are all body remains.

questions.question: Some fossils are parts of organisms that have not decayed. Why did they not decay?
options: One or more of the conditions needed for decay were absent
They were made of minerals when the organism was alive
markScheme: 1 mark: one or more of the conditions needed for decay were absent
questions.explanation: Decay needs warmth, moisture and oxygen. If any is missing, decomposers cannot break down the remains. Faster decomposer growth would speed up decay.

questions.question: Which part of an animal is most likely to be replaced by minerals to form a fossil?
markScheme: 1 mark: bones
questions.explanation: Hard parts such as bones, shells and teeth decay slowly, so there is time for minerals to replace them. Soft tissues such as skin, muscle and brain usually decay before this can happen.

questions.question: Which of these is an example of a fossil formed because the conditions for decay were absent?
options: A shell turned to stone by minerals
markScheme: 1 mark: an insect preserved in amber
questions.explanation: Amber keeps out oxygen and moisture, so the insect did not decay. Footprints and burrows are traces, and the stone shell was replaced by minerals.

questions.question: A woolly mammoth was found almost completely preserved in frozen ground in Siberia. Why had it not decayed?
options: Its bones had been replaced by minerals
It was too cold for decomposers to break it down
Mammoths do not contain any water
markScheme: 1 mark: it was too cold for decomposers to break it down
questions.explanation: Microorganisms need warmth to decay material. Light is not needed for decay, the mammoth was not mineralised, and its body did contain water.

questions.question: Why have the earliest forms of life left very few fossils?
options: They were soft-bodied, and traces were mainly destroyed by geological activity
They lived only on land where fossils cannot form
They were too large to be buried
They lived too recently to have formed fossils
markScheme: 1 mark: they were soft-bodied, and traces were destroyed by geological activity
questions.explanation: Soft bodies decay quickly and are rarely replaced by minerals, and geological activity destroyed most traces. Early life was microscopic or small and lived in water, and it is extremely old, not recent.

questions.question: What can scientists learn by comparing fossils of the same group of organisms from rocks of different ages?
options: How much or how little the organisms have changed over time
markScheme: 1 mark: how much or how little the organisms have changed over time
questions.explanation: Fossils show changes in structure over time. They rarely preserve colour or genes, and they cannot show exactly when life began because early life left few traces.

questions.question: Insects millions of years old can be found perfectly preserved in amber (hardened tree resin). Which explanation is correct?
options: The resin replaced the insect's body with minerals
The resin kept out oxygen and moisture, so decomposers could not decay the insect
The resin was hot, which killed the insect and stopped it decaying
The insect was a trace fossil left behind on the resin
markScheme: 1 mark: the resin kept out oxygen and moisture so decay could not happen
questions.explanation: Amber fossils are the organism itself, preserved because conditions for decay were absent. They are not mineral replacements or traces, and tree resin is not hot.

questions.question: On an evolutionary tree, species P and Q share a common ancestor from 2 million years ago, species R joins their branch at 10 million years ago, and species S joins at 30 million years ago. Which pair of species is most closely related?
markScheme: 1 mark: P and Q
questions.explanation: P and Q have the most recent common ancestor (2 million years ago), so they are most closely related. R joined 10 million years ago and S 30 million years ago, so they are more distantly related to P and Q.

questions.question: Fossils show that sharks have changed very little in hundreds of millions of years, whereas mammals have changed a great deal. Which is the best explanation?
options: Sharks do not have any genetic variation
Mammal fossils are easier to find, so they seem to change more
Sharks were already well adapted to a fairly stable environment, so there was little selection for change
markScheme: 1 mark: sharks were well adapted to a fairly stable environment so there was little selection for change
questions.explanation: When the environment stays similar and a species is already well suited to it, natural selection favours the existing characteristics. Sharks do have variation and do reproduce sexually.

questions.question: A fossil of one species is found in rock that is 140 million years old. A fossil of a related species is found in rock that is 65 million years old. Calculate the difference in age between the two fossils, in millions of years.
markScheme: 1 mark: 140 − 65 = 75 (million years)
questions.explanation: Subtract the younger age from the older age: 140 − 65 = 75 million years.

questions.question: Sediment builds up at the bottom of a lake at an average rate of 2 cm every 1000 years. A fossil fish is found 3 m below the top of the sediment. Estimate the age of the fossil in years.
questions.explanation: Convert metres to centimetres first. 300 cm ÷ 2 cm = 150 lots of 1000 years, which is 150 000 years. Forgetting to convert units gives 1500 years, which is wrong.

questions.question: Scientists identified 250 species of organism from fossils in one rock layer. 40 of these species were soft-bodied. Calculate the percentage of species that were soft-bodied.
questions.explanation: 40 ÷ 250 × 100 = 16%. This low percentage reflects how rarely soft-bodied organisms are preserved.

questions.question: On an evolutionary tree, species X and Y split from a common ancestor 12 million years ago. Species Y and Z split from a common ancestor 5 million years ago. How many million years before the Y and Z split did the X and Y split happen?
markScheme: 1 mark: 12 − 5 = 7 (million years)
questions.explanation: Both values are 'years ago', so subtract: 12 − 5 = 7 million years.

questions.question: Give two examples of preserved traces of organisms that can form fossils.
markScheme: 1 mark each, any two: footprints; burrows; rootlet traces
questions.explanation: These are the three examples of trace fossils named in the specification.

questions.question: In what are fossils usually found?
markScheme: 1 mark: rocks
questions.explanation: Fossils are found in rocks, usually sedimentary rocks formed from layers of mud or sand.

questions.question: Name two conditions that microorganisms need to decay dead organisms.
markScheme: 1 mark each, any two: warmth; moisture / water; oxygen
questions.explanation: If any of these is absent, decay stops or is very slow, which allows fossils of unchanged remains to form.

questions.question: Describe how a fossil of a bone can form by mineral replacement.
markScheme: 1 mark: the animal dies and is buried (quickly) in sediment
1 mark: soft parts decay but the bone decays slowly
1 mark: as the bone decays it is gradually replaced by minerals, forming a rock-like copy
questions.explanation: The key point is that minerals replace the bone as it decays. Burial in sediment protects the remains and supplies minerals in water.

questions.question: Explain why scientists cannot be certain about how life began on Earth.
markScheme: 1 mark: many early forms of life were soft-bodied so left few traces
1 mark: the traces that were left have mainly been destroyed by geological activity
questions.explanation: Both reasons together explain why there is very little fossil evidence from the earliest life.

questions.question: Suggest why fossils of jellyfish are much rarer than fossils of animals with shells.
markScheme: 1 mark: jellyfish are soft-bodied / have no hard parts
1 mark: soft tissue decays quickly so is rarely replaced by minerals, whereas shells decay slowly
questions.explanation: Mineral replacement needs time. Shells last long enough to be replaced; soft jellyfish bodies usually decay first.

questions.question: Bodies of animals that fell into acidic peat bogs thousands of years ago are sometimes found with skin and hair still present. Suggest why.
markScheme: 1 mark: peat bogs are acidic and have very little oxygen
1 mark: so microorganisms / decomposers cannot carry out decay, as conditions for decay are absent
questions.explanation: This is the 'conditions for decay absent' route. Lack of oxygen and acidic conditions stop decomposers working, so even soft tissue is preserved.

questions.question: Scientists use fossils of extinct organisms, as well as information about living organisms, to build evolutionary trees. Explain why fossil evidence is needed, and give one limitation of using fossils.
markScheme: 1 mark: fossils are the only evidence of extinct organisms / ancestors
1 mark: they show when organisms lived and how they changed, so branch points can be placed in time
1 mark: limitation: the fossil record is incomplete (soft-bodied organisms rarely fossilise / geological activity destroyed fossils), so some branches are uncertain
questions.explanation: Classification data come from living organisms, but fossils are needed for extinct ones. Gaps in the fossil record mean some relationships are based on limited evidence.

questions.question: A student finds a fossil footprint but no bones nearby. Suggest one piece of information the footprint can give scientists, and one piece it cannot.
markScheme: 1 mark: can show, e.g. size of the foot / animal, number of toes, whether it walked on two or four legs, how fast it moved
1 mark: cannot show, e.g. internal structure / skeleton, colour, exactly which species made it
questions.explanation: Trace fossils give evidence about behaviour and movement but not about the body itself.

questions.question: Describe the three ways in which fossils can be formed. Give an example of each.
markScheme: Indicative content: (1) parts of organisms do not decay because one or more conditions for decay (warmth, moisture, oxygen) are absent, e.g. mammoth in ice, insect in amber, body in peat bog; (2) parts of the organism are replaced by minerals as they decay, e.g. bones, shells, teeth buried in sediment become rock-like; (3) preserved traces of organisms, e.g. footprints, burrows, rootlet traces.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): all three ways described accurately, with correct examples for at least two.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or two ways described, or examples given with little description.
questions.explanation: Use the specification wording for each method and match each with a suitable example.

questions.question: Fossils provide evidence for the evolution of life on Earth. Evaluate the usefulness of the fossil record as evidence for evolution.
markScheme: Indicative content. Strengths: fossils are the remains of organisms from millions of years ago, found in rocks; deeper rock layers are usually older, so fossils can be put in order; they show how much or how little organisms have changed over time; simpler organisms appear in older rocks and more complex ones later; fossils are the only evidence of extinct organisms; they allow evolutionary trees to be drawn and dated; they can show gradual changes in structures. Limitations: the fossil record is incomplete; many early forms of life were soft-bodied so left few traces; many traces destroyed by geological activity; fossilisation needs particular conditions so is rare; we cannot be certain how life began; trace fossils give limited information. Conclusion: despite gaps, the fossils that exist show a consistent pattern of change and are strong evidence, especially combined with other evidence such as genes and antibiotic resistance.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a balanced evaluation with detailed strengths and limitations, and a justified conclusion.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): strengths and limitations described, but with less detail or no clear conclusion.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple points about fossils, mostly one-sided.
questions.explanation: An evaluate question needs both sides and a conclusion. Make sure each limitation is explained (why the record is incomplete), not just stated.

questions.question:
An evolutionary tree shows the following: a common ancestor lived 60 million years ago. Its descendants split into two lines 40 million years ago. In the first line, species A and B split 20 million years ago and both are alive today. In the second line, species C split off 30 million years ago and became extinct 10 million years ago; species D and E split 5 million years ago and both are alive today.
Use this information to compare how closely related the species are, and explain how scientists know species C existed.
markScheme: Indicative content: D and E are the most closely related (most recent common ancestor, 5 million years ago); A and B are closely related (common ancestor 20 million years ago) but less so than D and E; C is more closely related to D and E (common ancestor 30 million years ago) than to A or B (common ancestor 40 million years ago); A and B are equally related to C, D and E through the 40 million year branch point; C is extinct so is known only from fossils; fossils of C found in rocks dated between 30 and 10 million years old.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): correct comparisons using branch-point times, and explanation that C is known from fossil evidence.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): identifies one closely related pair or that C is known from fossils, with little explanation.
questions.explanation: Use the time of the most recent common ancestor to compare relatedness. Extinct species appear on trees because of fossil data.
